chapters.title: קִסְמֵי הָרַמַּאי הַגָּדוֹל
chapters.orig_title: The Magic Art of the Great Humbug

s.line: Next morning the Scarecrow said to his friends:
s.note: לְמָחֳרָת = "on the next day". With שֶׁ it becomes an adjective phrase: בַּבֹּקֶר שֶׁלְּמָחֳרָת (the morning of the next day), בַּיּוֹם שֶׁלְּמָחֳרָת (on the following day).

w: תַּגִּידוּ לִי מַזָּל טוֹב|congratulate me|~lit. say to me good luck
s.line: “Congratulate me.
s.note: מַזָּל טוֹב is what you say for any happy event: a birthday, a wedding, a new job. "To congratulate someone" is simply לְהַגִּיד (or לְאַחֵל) מַזָּל טוֹב. The formal verb is בֵּרֵךְ.

w: סוֹף סוֹף|at last|~idiom, lit. end end
s.line: I am going to Oz to get my brains at last.
When I return I shall be as other men are.”
s.note: After כְּשֶׁ ("when") about the future, Hebrew uses the future tense, unlike English: כְּשֶׁאֶחְזֹר = "when I (will) return". כְּשֶׁתַּגִּיעַ, תִּתְקַשֵּׁר = when you arrive, call.

s.line: “I have always liked you as you were,” said Dorothy simply.
“It is kind of you to like a Scarecrow,” he replied.
s.note: זֶה נֶחְמָד מִצִּדְּךָ / מִצִּדֵּךְ = "that's nice of you" (lit. "from your side"), an everyday phrase. The ending changes with the person addressed: מִצִּדְּךָ to a man, מִצִּדֵּךְ to a woman, as here to Dorothy.

s.line: “But surely you will think more of me when you hear the splendid thoughts my new brain is going to turn out.”
s.note: הֶעֱרִיךְ (hif'il) = to appreciate, and also to estimate: אֲנִי מַעֲרִיךְ אֶת הָעֶזְרָה שֶׁלְּךָ (I appreciate your help); מַעֲרִיכִים שֶׁ… (it is estimated that …) is common in the news. The noun is הַעֲרָכָה.

w: לַחֲדַר הַכֵּס|to the Throne Room|~lit. room of the throne
s.line: Then he said good-bye to them all in a cheerful voice and went to the Throne Room,
s.note: נִפְרַד מִ־ = to say goodbye to, to part from. It is a nif'al with an active meaning, and it takes מִ־. It also means "to separate" (a couple): הֵם נִפְרְדוּ = they broke up.

s.line: where he rapped upon the door.
“Come in,” said Oz.
s.note: תִּכָּנֵס is really the future ("you will come in"), but in speech the future is the normal way to give a request. The formal imperative הִכָּנֵס is used mostly in writing and on signs.

s.line: The Scarecrow went in and found the little man sitting down by the window,

w: שָׁקוּעַ בְּמַחְשָׁבוֹת|lost in thought|~idiom, lit. sunk in thoughts
s.line: engaged in deep thought.
s.note: שָׁקוּעַ בְּמַחְשָׁבוֹת = "lost in thought", lit. "sunk in thoughts". שָׁקוּעַ is the pa'ul form of שָׁקַע (to sink), and it is used for anyone absorbed in something: הוּא שָׁקוּעַ בָּעֲבוֹדָה (he is buried in work).

s.line: “I have come for my brains,” remarked the Scarecrow, a little uneasily.
s.note: אִי before a noun means "un-/non-": נוֹחוּת comfort → אִי נוֹחוּת discomfort, סֵדֶר order → אִי סֵדֶר disorder, הֲבָנָה understanding → אִי הֲבָנָה misunderstanding.

s.line: “Oh, yes; sit down in that chair, please,” replied Oz.
“You must excuse me for taking your head off,
s.note: מוֹרִיד לְךָ אֶת הָרֹאשׁ: for body parts Hebrew often says "to you the head" rather than "your head": הוּא שָׁבַר לִי אֶת הַיָּד (he broke my arm). Note also סָלַח לְ־: you forgive to someone. סְלִיחָה (sorry / excuse me) is from the same root.

s.line: but I shall have to do it in order to put your brains in their proper place.”
s.note: הִצְטָרֵךְ = "to need to, to have to". In hitpa'el, when the root starts with צ, the ת of the prefix swaps places with it and turns into ט: not *הִתְצָרֵךְ but הִצְטָרֵךְ. The same happens in מִצְטַעֵר (sorry).

s.line: “That’s all right,” said the Scarecrow.
“You are quite welcome to take my head off,
s.note: בְּשִׂמְחָה ("with joy") is the everyday "gladly / you're welcome to": — אֶפְשָׁר לָשֶׁבֶת? — בְּשִׂמְחָה! (May I sit? Please do!).

s.line: as long as it will be a better one when you put it on again.”
s.note: כָּל עוֹד = "as long as", both in time and as a condition: כָּל עוֹד אַתָּה כָּאן (as long as you're here). הֶחְזִיר (hif'il of חָזַר, to return) = to give back, to put back.

s.line: So the Wizard unfastened his head and emptied out the straw.
s.note: פֵּרֵק (pi'el) = to take apart, to dismantle: לְפָרֵק אֶת הָאָרוֹן (to take the closet apart). You will also see it in the news: פֵּרוּק נֶשֶׁק (disarmament).

s.line: Then he entered the back room and took up a measure of bran,
which he mixed with a great many pins and needles.
s.note: סִכָּה = a pin (also a hair clip or a brooch: סִכַּת בִּטָּחוֹן is a safety pin). מַחַט = a needle. It is feminine even though its plural is מְחָטִים.

s.line: Having shaken them together thoroughly,
he filled the top of the Scarecrow’s head with the mixture and stuffed the rest of the space with straw, to hold it in place.
s.note: תַּעֲרֹבֶת (a mixture) comes from the same root as עִרְבֵּב (to mix). Note also מִלֵּא X בְּ־ Y = to fill X with Y, and הֵיטֵב = "well, thoroughly", a slightly higher word than טוֹב: הַקְשִׁיבוּ הֵיטֵב (listen carefully).

s.line: When he had fastened the Scarecrow’s head on his body again he said to him,
“Hereafter you will be a great man, for I have given you a lot of bran-new brains.”
s.note: Baum's joke: "bran-new" sounds like "brand-new". Hebrew says "brand-new" as חָדָשׁ מֵהַנַּיְלוֹן ("new from the nylon", i.e. still in its plastic wrap), so חָדָשׁ מֵהַסֻּבִּין ("new from the bran") keeps the pun.

s.line: The Scarecrow was both pleased and proud at the fulfillment of his greatest wish,
s.note: הִתְגַּשֵּׁם = to come true: הַחֲלוֹם שֶׁלִּי הִתְגַּשֵּׁם (my dream came true). מְרֻצֶּה (pleased, satisfied) is a pu'al participle, like מְאֻשָּׁר; לָקוֹחַ מְרֻצֶּה is a satisfied customer.

s.line: and having thanked Oz warmly he went back to his friends.
s.note: הוֹדָה לְ־ = to thank (someone), the verb behind תּוֹדָה. With בְּ־ the same verb means "to admit": הוּא הוֹדָה בָּאַשְׁמָה (he admitted the charge), common in news reports.

s.line: Dorothy looked at him curiously.
His head was quite bulged out at the top with brains.
s.note: תָּפוּחַ here is the pa'ul form of תָּפַח (to swell): "swollen". Written the same way, תַּפּוּחַ is an apple, but the vowels and the dagesh differ. מֵרֹב + noun = "from so much …": מֵרֹב עֲבוֹדָה (from all the work), מֵרֹב צְחוֹק (from laughing so hard).

s.line: “How do you feel?” she asked.
“I feel wise indeed,” he answered earnestly.
“When I get used to my brains I shall know everything.”
s.note: הִתְרַגֵּל לְ־ = to get used to: הִתְרַגַּלְתִּי לַחֹם (I got used to the heat). It is related to הֶרְגֵּל (a habit) and רָגִיל (usual, used to). Note again the future after כְּשֶׁ.

s.line: “Why are those needles and pins sticking out of your head?” asked the Tin Woodman.
s.note: בּוֹלְטוֹת is feminine plural because both מַחַט and סִכָּה are feminine. בָּלַט = to stick out, and also "to stand out": הִיא בּוֹלֶטֶת בַּכִּתָּה (she stands out in class).

s.line: “That is proof that he is sharp,” remarked the Lion.
s.note: The Lion's joke works in Hebrew too: חַד means "sharp" (a knife, a needle) and also "quick-witted": הוּא בָּחוּר חַד (he's a sharp guy). חַד also means "clear-cut": תְּשׁוּבָה חַדָּה.

s.line: “Well, I must go to Oz and get my heart,” said the Woodman.
So he walked to the Throne Room and knocked at the door.
“Come in,” called Oz,
and the Woodman entered and said,
“I have come for my heart.”
“Very well,” answered the little man.
“But I shall have to cut a hole in your breast, so I can put your heart in the right place.
I hope it won’t hurt you.”
s.note: כָּאַב לְ־: in Hebrew the thing that hurts is the subject, and the person gets לְ־: כּוֹאֵב לִי הָרֹאשׁ (my head hurts, lit. "the head hurts to me"), זֶה כּוֹאֵב לְךָ? (does it hurt you?).

s.line: “Oh, no,” answered the Woodman.
“I shall not feel it at all.”
So Oz brought a pair of tinsmith’s shears and cut a small, square hole in the left side of the Tin Woodman’s breast.
s.note: מִסְפָּרַיִם (scissors) has the dual ending ַיִם, so "a pair of" is built in, as in מִשְׁקָפַיִם (glasses). פֶּחָח (tinsmith, from פַּח) has the pattern of trades like נַגָּר (carpenter) and טַבָּח (cook); because ח cannot take a dagesh, the first vowel changes. In Israel a פֶּחָח today is the person who fixes car bodywork.

s.line: Then, going to a chest of drawers,
he took out a pretty heart, made entirely of silk and stuffed with sawdust.
s.note: Two passive participles: עָשׂוּי מִ־ (pa'ul) = "made of": עָשׂוּי מֵעֵץ (made of wood); מְמֻלָּא (pu'al, from pi'el מִלֵּא) = stuffed, filled. פִּלְפֵּל מְמֻלָּא (stuffed pepper) is a common dish.

s.line: “Isn’t it a beauty?” he asked.
s.note: יְפֵהפֶה (fem. יְפֵהפִיָּה) is a doubled form of יָפֶה, meaning "very beautiful". A question with לֹא asks for agreement, like English "isn't it?".

s.line: “It is, indeed!” replied the Woodman, who was greatly pleased.
“But is it a kind heart?”
“Oh, very!” answered Oz.
He put the heart in the Woodman’s breast and then replaced the square of tin,
soldering it neatly together where it had been cut.
s.note: נֶחְתַּךְ is the nif'al of חָתַךְ (to cut), used as a passive: "was cut". Compare נֶחְפַּר (was dug). בְּקַפְּדָנוּת = carefully, meticulously; a קַפְּדָן is a stickler.

s.line: “There,” said he;
“now you have a heart that any man might be proud of.
s.note: גֵּאֶה בְּ־ = proud of: אֲנִי גֵּאֶה בָּךְ (I'm proud of you). הָיָה + participle or adjective can mean "would": כָּל אָדָם הָיָה גֵּאֶה = any man would be proud.

s.line: I’m sorry I had to put a patch on your breast,

w: לֹא הָיְתָה בְּרֵרָה|there was no choice|~idiom
s.line: but it really couldn’t be helped.”
s.note: אֵין בְּרֵרָה (past: לֹא הָיְתָה בְּרֵרָה) = "there's no choice", one of the most common phrases in Israeli Hebrew. Note הָיְתָה, feminine, agreeing with בְּרֵרָה.

s.line: “Never mind the patch,” exclaimed the happy Woodman.
s.note: עֲזֹב (lit. "leave") is everyday for "never mind, forget it": עֲזֹב, זֶה לֹא חָשׁוּב. In speech you'll mostly hear the future form תַּעֲזֹב (to a woman תַּעַזְבִי).

w: אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה|grateful|~idiom, lit. prisoner of thanks
s.line: “I am very grateful to you, and shall never forget your kindness.”
s.note: אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה ("a prisoner of thanks") = deeply grateful, a slightly formal set phrase (fem. אֲסִירַת תּוֹדָה). לְעוֹלָם לֹא = never (about the future): לְעוֹלָם לֹא אֶשְׁכַּח.

w: אֵין עַל מָה|don't mention it|~idiom, lit. there is nothing for what
s.line: “Don’t speak of it,” replied Oz.
s.note: אֵין עַל מָה = "you're welcome / don't mention it", the standard answer to תּוֹדָה. Also common: בְּכֵיף (slang, "with pleasure").

s.line: Then the Tin Woodman went back to his friends,
who wished him every joy on account of his good fortune.
s.note: אִחֵל לְ־ = to wish (someone something): אִחַלְתִּי לָהּ הַצְלָחָה. לְרֶגֶל = "on the occasion of", a higher-register word seen in invitations and the news: לְרֶגֶל יוֹם הַהֻלֶּדֶת, סָגוּר לְרֶגֶל שִׁפּוּצִים (closed for renovations).

s.line: The Lion now walked to the Throne Room and knocked at the door.
“Come in,” said Oz.
“I have come for my courage,” announced the Lion, entering the room.
s.note: הִכְרִיז (hif'il) = to announce, to declare, a word you will meet constantly in the news: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה הִכְרִיזָה עַל… (the government announced …). The noun is הַכְרָזָה, and a כָּרוֹז is a town crier or a leaflet.

s.line: “Very well,” answered the little man;
“I will get it for you.”
He went to a cupboard and reaching up to a high shelf took down a square green bottle,
s.note: הוֹשִׁיט יָד = to reach out (a hand). It is also used figuratively: לְהוֹשִׁיט יָד לְשָׁלוֹם (to extend a hand for peace) is a stock phrase in political speeches. נִגַּשׁ לְ־ = to go up to, to approach; in the infinitive it is לָגֶשֶׁת.

s.line: the contents of which he poured into a green-gold dish, beautifully carved.
s.note: לְהַפְלִיא ("to amaze") is used as an adverb, "wonderfully, remarkably": הִיא שָׁרָה לְהַפְלִיא (she sings wonderfully). מְגֻלֶּפֶת is a pu'al participle, "carved", from pi'el גִּלֵּף. Note the word order: the object אֶת הַתֹּכֶן comes first for emphasis, which אֶת makes clear.

w: מָצְאָה חֵן בְּעֵינָיו|he liked|~idiom, lit. found favor in his eyes
s.line: Placing this before the Cowardly Lion, who sniffed at it as if he did not like it,
s.note: מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי ("found favor in the eyes of") is the normal way to say "to like" something: הַסֶּרֶט מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינַי (I liked the movie). The thing liked is the subject, so here the verb is feminine to agree with קְעָרָה.

s.line: the Wizard said:
“Drink.”
“What is it?” asked the Lion.
“Well,” answered Oz,
“if it were inside of you, it would be courage.
s.note: An unreal condition: אִם + past, then הָיָה in the main clause = "if it were …, it would be …". More careful Hebrew uses אִלּוּ or לוּ for this, but אִם is what most people say.

s.line: You know, of course, that courage is always inside one;
s.note: הֲרֵי = "after all, as you know", a little word that appeals to something both speakers agree on: הֲרֵי אָמַרְתִּי לְךָ (I told you, didn't I). נִמְצָא = "is (located)", nif'al with an active sense, as in אֵיפֹה נִמְצָא הַבַּנְק?

s.line: so that this really cannot be called courage until you have swallowed it.
s.note: English "cannot be called" is passive; Hebrew prefers an impersonal active phrase, אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִקְרֹא לָזֶה ("one cannot call it"). Note also קָרָא לְ־ = to call (by a name): קוֹרְאִים לִי דָּנִי (my name is Danny).

w: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר|as soon as possible|~idiom, lit. as much as more quickly
s.line: Therefore I advise you to drink it as soon as possible.”
s.note: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר + adverb/adjective = "as … as possible": כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר (ASAP), כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר זוֹל (as cheap as possible). הִמְלִיץ = to recommend, advise; הַמְלָצָה is a recommendation or a reference letter.

s.line: The Lion hesitated no longer,
but drank till the dish was empty.
s.note: הִסֵּס (pi'el) = to hesitate; בְּלִי לְהַסֵּס = without hesitating, and הִסּוּס = hesitation. Here לֹא … יוֹתֵר = "no longer": הוּא לֹא גָּר פֹּה יוֹתֵר (he doesn't live here anymore).

s.line: “How do you feel now?” asked Oz.
“Full of courage,” replied the Lion,
who went joyfully back to his friends to tell them of his good fortune.
s.note: סִפֵּר לְ־ … עַל … = to tell someone about something. In pa'al the same root gives סָפַר, "to count", and סֵפֶר is a book.

s.line: Oz, left to himself,
smiled to think of his success in giving the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman and the Lion exactly what they thought they wanted.
s.note: חָשְׁבוּ שֶׁהֵם רוֹצִים: after verbs of thinking and saying, Hebrew keeps the tense of the original thought, so "they thought they wanted" is literally "they thought that they want". The same in הוּא אָמַר שֶׁהוּא עָיֵף (he said he was tired).

s.line: “How can I help being a humbug,” he said,
“when all these people make me do things that everybody knows can’t be done?
s.note: גָּרַם לְ־ + infinitive = to make (someone do something), to cause: הַסֶּרֶט גָּרַם לִי לִבְכּוֹת (the movie made me cry). Note also כֻּלָּם יוֹדְעִים: כֻּלָּם "everybody" takes a plural verb.

s.line: It was easy to make the Scarecrow and the Lion and the Woodman happy, because they imagined I could do anything.
s.note: שִׂמֵּחַ (pi'el) = to make happy, the causative of pa'al שָׂמַח (to be happy). Pi'el often works this way: גָּדַל grew → גִּדֵּל raised. דִּמְיֵן (to imagine) is a four-letter root, from דִּמְיוֹן (imagination), which appears in the next sentence.

w: יִהְיֶה צָרִיךְ|it will take|~impersonal: it will be necessary
s.line: But it will take more than imagination to carry Dorothy back to Kansas,
and I’m sure I don’t know how it can be done.”
s.note: אֵין לִי מוּשָׂג = "I have no idea", very common. Baum's "I'm sure I don't know" is an old emphatic way of saying the same. עוֹשִׂים with no subject is the impersonal "one does / it is done": אֵיךְ עוֹשִׂים אֶת זֶה? (how is it done?).
